name: Chechen
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it). One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Dotton & Wagner 2017 2017.
catalog_quote: Chechen stress is primarily fixed on the first syllable of a phonological word. Stress in Chechen is also often realized by a raising of the tone on a stressed syllable rather than an increase in the intensity (cf English and Russian stress-timed systems).
sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Chechen: Komen 2007 (ROA-923), already in our bibliography and already held held by the project (copied into this search of works with stress in the title directory, byte-identical to the live ROA PDF athttps://roa.rutgers.edu/files/923-0807/923-KOMEN-0-0.PDF;the old view.php3 landing page is 404). Read in full: main stress on the first syllable of a left-aligned trochaic foot, weight-insensitive, cued by highest pitch; exceptions are preverb compounds (separate prosodic words), list/focus intonation, and inherent high tone on a few suffixes. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict coding (deciding source Dotton & Wagner 2017, previously confirmed verbatim in the held grammar) and does not supersede it, though it is the stronger first-hand study. Nothing new to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title; the standing list of works to obtain (Nichols 1997 'Chechen phonology', Komen/Molochieva/Nichols 2020 OUP chapter) is unchanged. none were needed for this single-item search.

new_statements.quote: It has been shown that the main stress in Chechen usually lies on the first syllable of the word. Chechen stress uses trochaic feet. These feet should start as much to the left as possible. There is downstep between feet [...]. Inherent high tone on certain morphemes, as well as intonation are able to break up the normal stress assignment pattern. [...] Chechen does not seem to distinguish between light and heavy syllables when it comes to stress assignment.
new_statements.citation: Komen, Erwin R. (2007). Chechen stress and vowel deletion: an optimality theory approach. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-923, 19 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 18, sec. 6 'Conclusions' (first-syllable statement); p. 3, sec. 3 (trochaic/leftmost tendencies); p. 19 (weight-insensitivity)
new_statements.reading: First-hand elicitation with pitch tracks: word stress is initial (leftmost trochee, weight-insensitive), realised as the highest tone. Departures are morphological/prosodic, not lexical-contrastive: preverb+verb compounds behave as two prosodic words (preverb stressed separately, per Nichols 1997:966), list/focus intonation adds a final high tone, and a few suffix combinations (e.g. past + question /-írii/) carry inherent high tone that draws prominence to the penult. Consistent with the catalog's fixed-strict coding; if the catalog distinguishes strict from 'fixed with morphological exceptions', the preverb double-stress and suffix-tone cases are the caveats to note.

new_statements.quote: That the first syllable of a phonological phrase starts with a high tone is usual, since, as far as stress in Chechen is concerned, it has been established that Chechen uses trochees with the main stress of the word's first trochee (Komen 2007). The fact that Chechen uses trochees (feet with the main stress on the first syllable) explains why marking the last syllable of the phonological phrase preceding the focused constituent with a high tone is so discernable – it overrules the normal rules of stress assignment.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (fixed-strict, initial: 'Chechen stress is primarily fixed on the first syllable of a phonological word.. realized by a raising of the tone') and as the existing Komen 2007 ROA-923 statement (leftmost trochee, stress = high tone). Adds only phrase-level focus prosody (pre-focus final-syllable high tone), which is intonational, not a word-stress exception.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is initial: Chechen builds trochaic feet and the main stress is the head of the word's first trochee (first syllable), realized as a high tone; the thesis takes this as established (citing the author's own 2007 stress paper, ROA-923) and uses it as the baseline against which focus prosody is described. Focus adds phrase-level marking: the focused constituent's first syllable carries the high tone and the LAST syllable of the preceding phonological phrase is also stressed/high, which the author describes as overruling normal (initial, trochaic) stress assignment; an unmarked SOV clause keeps the trochaic structure in one prosodic phrase with decreasing tone. The negator ca never bears stress (treated as a clitic on the verb).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied by the trochaic-foot statement (further trochees after the first carry lesser stresses; appendix 10.1 transcriptions mark 'other stresses' with acute and grave accents), but no explicit rule for secondary stress placement is stated in this work.
new_statements.exceptions: Phrase-level only: under focus the final syllable of the phrase preceding the focused constituent is stressed (high tone), overriding word-level initial stress; one elicited clause (ex. 30) lacks this pre-focus final stress; the negation particle is never stressed. No lexical exceptions to initial word stress are given here (the work refers to Komen 2007 'Chechen stress and vowel deletion' for the stress analysis).
new_statements.identity_note: Standard/literary Chechen as spoken by the author's consultant(s) (elicited focus paradigm and two transcribed narratives; thesis written at Leiden with SIL; no dialect named in the prosody section).

sources.quote: "In Chechen, stress is fixed on the first syllable. According to Magomedov (2005: 86), long vowels can attract stress away from the initial position, but this view is not shared by other authors. Exceptionally, though Chechen does not have strong evidence for secondary stress, verbs that take preverbs carry stress both on the preverb and on the verbal root (Nichols 1997: 966; Komen 2007a: 8)." Later: enclitic ʔa "can in certain cases attract stress, shifting it to the final syllable of the word (Nichols 1997: 967)"; proclitics t͡sa, ma carry H tone but do not attract stress.

tone.quote: This article deals with the speech melody of speech-raising and lowering the tone in the narrative, interrogative, motivational and exclamation sentences of the Chechen language. … In the Chechen language the descending intonation is used in narrative, interrogative, motivational, and exclamation sentences. In the intonation-interrogative sentences the ascending-descending intonation is used at the beginning of sentences and high pitch on the penultimate word with a gradual descent of the tone at the end of the sentence.

tone.quote: Г.А. Климов пишет о том, что «ударение в большинстве нахско-дагестанских языков должно быть охарактеризовано как слабо выраженное динамическое и разноместное», с уточнением, что «в ряде случаев – особенно отчетливо дающих о себе знать в авароандоцезском ареале – трудности определения его позиции обусловлены его сложным взаимодействием с тоновыми различиями» [21, с. 89]. Распространим это высказывание и на чеченский язык, характеризующийся и сложностью вокализма, и фонематическим противопоставлением гласных по степени долготы.
tone.locator: p. 114 (body, unsectioned; sentence opens bottom of p. 113)
tone.translation: G. A. Klimov writes that 'stress in most Nakh-Daghestanian languages must be characterised as weakly expressed, dynamic and free', specifying that 'in a number of cases, most clearly in the Avar-Andi-Tsez area, the difficulty of determining its position is due to its complex interaction with tonal differences' [21, p. 89]. Let us extend this statement to Chechen as well, which is characterised both by a complex vowel system and by a phonemic opposition of vowels by degree of length.
tone.summary: Weighs dynamic, tonal (musical) and quantitative accent; argues Chechen has no dynamic stress, only a vowel-length opposition; tone enters only via Klimov's areal remark, with no tone analysis.
tone.says: Weighs dynamic, tonal (musical) and quantitative accent; argues Chechen has no dynamic stress, only a vowel-length opposition; tone enters only via Klimov's areal remark, with no tone analysis.
